text: The Kusumbai Motichand Planetarium, the first projection planetarium in Asia, became operational at the New English School in Pune on 18 September 1954. It was named after the mother of Seth Motichand Shah, son-in-law of Seth Walchand Hirachand (1882–1953), the founder of the Walchand group of Industries. The project was made possible by a generous donation of Rs.50,000 from the Walchand Group in the early 1950s. The planetarium movement in India began with the opening of this simple planetarium at the New English School in Pune in 1954. The school building features a unique Y-shaped architecture with three linear wings connected at a 120-degree angle to a central hub. The topmost point of the hub is a concrete hemispherical dome, approximately 9 metres (30 ft) in inner diameter, housing the planetarium. The floor area is 63 square meters, and the facility can accommodate 100 people at a time. The planetarium was inaugurated by Girija Shankar Bajpai, the then Governor of Bombay Province. The concept of simulating planetary motions against an artificial night sky originated in 1913 when German astronomer Max Wolf suggested it to German engineer Oskar von Miller, founder president of the Deutsches Museum in Munich. Planetarium Jena, the oldest continuously operating planetarium in the world, first used this projector technology in 1926. After the first modern planetarium, planetariums were established in Europe, Japan, and America over the next twenty years, but not in India. In the late 1930s, Armand Spitz, a part-time lecturer at The Fels Planetarium of the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia, developed his own projector for affordable planetariums. While designing the projector, he encountered difficulties with the icosahedron-shaped globe and sought help from Albert Einstein, who suggested using a dodecahedron. Spitz successfully implemented this design, producing an inexpensive projector that is believed to be the only one in the world still operating its shows with this technology for over sixty years. The Kusumbai Motichand Planetarium is equipped with a Spitz A1 projector imported from Philadelphia, making it the oldest operational planetarium instrument in India. Since 2004, the projector remained out of order, leading to a suspension of shows. In 2012, staff from New English School undertook efforts to revive the planetarium by replacing defective components such as the transformer, mercury switches, projector motor, and electrical bulbs. Modifications were also made to the projection system to display zodiacs. After seven years of non-operation, the planetarium was reopened to the public on 28 February 2012, the occasion of National Science Day. It is considered the oldest functional school planetarium in Asia.
